title: Differential diagnosis and treatment of wide QRS tachycardia in an Ebstein anomaly patient
case_prompt:
A 20-year-old man with a known diagnosis of asymptomatic Ebstein anomaly presented to the emergency department with palpitations and dizziness. On examination, he had skin pallor, cyanosis, diaphoresis, and a heart rate of 188 beats per minute. An electrocardiogram showed a wide QRS complex tachycardia, and the patient underwent immediate electrical cardioversion. After restoration of sinus rhythm, the ECG demonstrated an intraventricular conduction delay.

Transthoracic echocardiography revealed apical displacement of the septal and posterior tricuspid leaflets consistent with Ebstein anomaly, severe tricuspid regurgitation, “atrialization” of a large portion of the right ventricle, and right ventricular dysfunction. Coronary computed tomographic angiography showed no coronary obstruction. Cardiac magnetic resonance imaging confirmed a septal tricuspid leaflet apical displacement of 33 mm relative to the mitral valve plane, elongated and redundant tricuspid leaflets leading to severe regurgitation, a right atrial plus atrialized right ventricular volume of 120 mL, an end-diastolic right ventricular volume of 125 mL (34 mL atrialized), and a right ventricular ejection fraction of 37% without late gadolinium enhancement.

The patient was referred for an electrophysiology study and catheter ablation.
diagnostic_reasoning:
1. Atrial tachycardia was excluded because “V-V interval modification preceded A-A modification, ruling out atrial tachycardia as the mechanism of arrhythmia.”  
2. An accessory pathway was deemed improbable on baseline electrophysiology, since “para-His pacing showed an increase in VA interval with His capture loss and apical programmed ventricular stimulation showing an increase in VA interval during retrograde right bundle branch block.”  
3. Orthodromic atrioventricular reentrant tachycardia was excluded because “there was no VA activation change during aberrancy recovery, and no atrial timing modification during refractory His pacing, suggesting that orthodromic AV reentrant tachycardia was not the mechanism of arrhythmia.”  
4. Atrioventricular nodal reentrant tachycardia was considered most probable after eliminating other supraventricular mechanisms: “we interpreted that AV nodal reentrant tachycardia was the most probable mechanism of arrhythmia.”  
5. Ventricular tachycardia was confirmed for the second wide complex tachycardia by entrainment maneuvers, as “atrial entrainment maneuver showed QRS fusion and an AVVA response; this maneuver confirms ventricular tachycardia as the mechanism of the second tachycardia.”
